'''Antoine Y. Song''' (born 18 July 1992 in Paris) is a French<ref name="cv">{{Cite web|url=https://web.math.princeton.edu/~aysong/moncv.pdf|title=Song's CV}}</ref> mathematician whose research concerns [[differential geometry]] and [[geometric analysis]]. He is a professor at [[Caltech]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://pma.caltech.edu/people/antoine-song | title=Antoine Song &#124; the Division of Physics, Mathematics and Astronomy }}</ref> In 2018, he proved [[Yau's conjecture]].

== Education ==
Antoine Song was a student at the [[École normale supérieure (Paris)|École Normale Supérieure de Paris]] from 2012 to 2015. He obtained a bachelor's and a master's degree in mathematics from the [[Pierre and Marie Curie University|Université Pierre et Marie Curie]] (Paris 6).<ref name="cv" /> He obtained his Ph.D. from [[Princeton University]] in 2019 under the supervision of [[Fernando Codá Marques]], with the thesis ''In search of minimal hypersurfaces''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=252005}}</ref>

== Mathematical work ==

It is known that any closed surface possesses infinitely many [[closed geodesic]]s. The first problem in the minimal submanifolds section of [[Shing-Tung Yau|Yau]]'s list ([[Yau's conjecture]]) asks whether  any closed [[three-manifold]] has infinitely many closed smooth [[Immersion (mathematics)#Immersed plane curves|immersed]] minimal surfaces. At the time it was known from [[Almgren–Pitts min-max theory]] the existence of at least one minimal surface. Kei Irie, [[Fernando Codá Marques]], and [[André Neves]] solved this problem in the [[Generic property|generic]] case <ref>{{cite journal | last1=Irie | first1=Kei | last2=Marques | first2=Fernando | last3=Neves | first3=André | title=Density of minimal hypersurfaces for generic metrics | journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] | date=2018 | volume=187 | issue=3 | doi=10.4007/annals.2018.187.3.8}}</ref> and later Song proved it in full generality.{{sfn|Song|2023}}

Together with Conghan Dong,{{sfn|Dong|Song|2025}} he proved a conjecture from 2001 by [[Gerhard Huisken|G. Huisken]] and [[Tom Ilmanen|T. Ilmanen]] on the mathematics of [[general relativity]], about the [[curvature]] in spaces with very little [[mass]].<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/a-century-later-new-math-smooths-out-general-relativity-20231130/|title=A Century Later, New Math Smooths Out General Relativity|magazine=[[Quanta Magazine]]|date=30 November 2023|first=Steve|last=Nadis}}</ref>

==Honours and awards==
He was a [[Clay Mathematics Institute|Clay Research Fellow]] (2019–2024).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.claymath.org/people/antoine-song|title=Antoine Song &#124; Clay Mathematics Institute|website=www.claymath.org}}</ref>

He is a [[Sloan Research Fellowship|Sloan Fellow]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/caltech-professors-win-2024-sloan-fellowships | title=Caltech Professors Win 2024 Sloan Fellowships | date=20 February 2024 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://sloan.org/fellowships/2024-Fellows | title=2024 Fellows &#124; Alfred P. Sloan Foundation }}</ref>

He delivered the 2021–2022 [[Peccot Lectures]] (in 2022, due to the coronavirus pandemic).<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.insmi.cnrs.fr/fr/cnrsinfo/cours-peccot-2021-2022 | title=Cours Peccot 2021-2022 &#124; CNRS Mathématiques | date=27 September 2021 }}</ref>

In 2024, he received the ''Frontiers of Science Award''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.insmi.cnrs.fr/en/cnrsinfo/prix-frontiers-of-science-2024|title=Twenty French mathematicians win Frontiers of Science 2024 prize (Beijing) &#124; CNRS Mathématiques|date=July 14, 2024|website=www.insmi.cnrs.fr}}</ref>
